subject: Biology
central_question: How are tissues organised internally in flowering-plant roots, stems, and leaves, and how do monocot and dicot structures differ?
in_scope_units: The epidermal tissue system, including epidermis, cuticle, stomata, guard cells, subsidiary cells, root hairs, and trichomes.
The ground tissue system and the distribution of parenchyma, collenchyma, sclerenchyma, and mesophyll.
The vascular tissue system, including xylem, phloem, radial and conjoint arrangements, and open and closed vascular bundles.
Internal organisation of dicotyledonous and monocotyledonous roots.
Internal organisation of dicotyledonous and monocotyledonous stems.
Internal organisation of dorsiventral dicot leaves and isobilateral monocot leaves.
banned_topics: Detailed secondary growth beyond the brief references in the chapter
Physiological mechanisms of transpiration and photosynthesis
Cell division and molecular differentiation of tissues

known_pitfalls.correction: The cuticle commonly covers aerial epidermis but is absent in roots.
Dicot guard cells are generally bean-shaped, whereas grasses have dumb-bell-shaped guard cells.

known_pitfalls.claim: Every vascular bundle containing xylem and phloem is open.
known_pitfalls.correction: Open bundles contain cambium; closed bundles lack cambium.

known_pitfalls.claim: Dicot and monocot roots differ only externally.
known_pitfalls.correction: They differ anatomically in xylem number, pith development, and secondary-growth potential.

known_pitfalls.claim: Monocot stems have vascular bundles arranged in a ring.
known_pitfalls.correction: Monocot stem bundles are numerous and scattered; dicot stem bundles form a ring.

known_pitfalls.claim: Both leaf types have palisade and spongy mesophyll.
known_pitfalls.correction: Dorsiventral dicot leaves are differentiated; isobilateral monocot mesophyll is generally undifferentiated.
